quote_evidence: ἀπάντων δὴ τῶν γινομένων Ἀριστοτέλης ποιούμενος τὴν διαίρεσιν τὰ μὲν αὐτῶν τινος χάριν γίνεσθαι λέγει σκοπόν τινα καὶ τέλος τῶν γινομένων προκείμενον ἔχοντος τοῦ ποιοῦντος αὐτά, τὰ δὲ οὐδενός.

quote_evidence: εἰσὶ δέ τινες οἵ φασιν, οἷον οἱ Μεγαρικοί, ὅταν ἐνεργῇ μόνον δύνασθαι, ὅταν δὲ μὴ ἐνεργῇ οὐ δύνασθαι

quote_evidence: Τούτων γὰρ ἀνάγκη μὲν θάτερον μόριον τῆς ἀντιφάσεως ἀληθὲς εἶναι ἢ ψεῦδος, οὐ μέντοι τόδε ἢ τόδε ἀλλ᾿ ὁπότερ᾿ ἔτυχε

quote_evidence: Ἄμα γὰρ δυνατὸν εἶναι καὶ μὴ εἶναι· εἰ δ᾿ ἀνάγκη εἶναι ἢ μὴ εἶναι, οὐκ ἔσται δυνατὸν ἄμφω.

rationale: The node's key textual anchor is DI 9, 18a31-32, where Aristotle has 'already established that one can assume PB without assuming RCP': for universals not stated universally, it is NOT necessary that one statement be true and the other false. rationale: Phil 2:13 is Eastman's flagship text for participatory, relationally constituted agency: even willing (τὸ θέλειν) and working are energized by God working within — agency embedded in relation to a divine other rather than self-originating.

quote_evidence: Λέγω δὲ οἷον ἀνάγκη μὲν ἔσεσθαι ναυμαχίαν αὔριον ἢ μὴ ἔσεσθαι, οὐ μέντοι ἔσεσθαί γε αὔριον ναυμαχίαν ἀναγκαῖον οὐδὲ μὴ γενέσθαι· γενέσθαι μέντοι ἢ μὴ γενέσθαι ἀναγκαῖον.
rationale: Aristotle, De Interpretatione 9, 19a30-32 (corpus ref 9.15): the exact sea-battle sentence and Aristotle's solution — the disjunction is necessary but neither disjunct is individually necessary. This is precisely the claim stated by the node.

rationale: De Interpretatione 9, 18a28-18b25 (corpus ref 9.2): the deterministic argument from bivalence over future singulars that Aristotle sets up, ending with the first occurrence of the sea-battle example — the problem the node describes.

rationale: Ammonius, In De Interpretatione 154 (newly ingested): late-antique commentary explicitly expounding Aristotle's sea-battle solution (whole antiphasis necessary, neither part determinately). Evidences the node's claim that the text became central to later debates on future contingents.

quote_evidence: τὸ ἀξίωμα τὸ ἔσται αὔριον ναυμαχία ἀληθὲς μὲν εἶναι δύνασθαι, οὐ μέντοι καὶ ἀναγκαῖον

quote_evidence: Acutius Carneades, qui docebat posse Epicureos suam causam sine hac commenticia declinatione defendere. Nam cum docerent esse posse quendam animi motum voluntarium, id fuit defendi melius quam introducere declinationem, cuius praesertim causam reperire non possent; quo defenso facile Chrysippo possent resistere.
rationale: Cicero, De Fato 23 — the principal source Fürst himself names (De Fato 23-25). Cicero's testimonium of Carneades' 'animi motus voluntarius' against Chrysippus, including the denial of external antecedent causes of volition ('voluntatis enim nostrae non esse causas externas et antecedentis' follows in the same passage).

quote_evidence: Similiter ad animorum motus voluntarios non est requirenda externa causa; motus enim voluntarius eam naturam in se ipse continet, ut sit in nostra potestate nobisque pareat, nec id sine causa; eius rei enim causa ipsa natura est.
rationale: Cicero, De Fato 25: the completion of the Carneadean argument — voluntary motion contains its nature in itself ('in se ipse continet'), is in our power, and is its own cause. Directly evidences the node's 'cause sui de la décision' / willentliche Selbstbewegung claim.

quote_evidence: καίτοι δεῖ, τριῶν ὄντων, ἢ μὴ πᾶσαν εἶναι φαντασίαν εἱμαρμένης ἔργον ἢ πᾶσαν παραδοχὴν φαντασίας καὶ συγκατάθεσιν ἀναμάρτητον ἢ μηδʼ αὐτὴν τὴν εἱμαρμένην ἀνεπίληπτον
rationale: Plutarch, De Stoicorum repugnantiis 47 (≈1056E-1057C) — the parallel locus the node itself cites ('= Plutarque, Stoic. Repugn. 1057-58'). Preserves the Academic anti-Chrysippean trilemma that assent cannot both be fate's work (via phantasia) and blameworthy, the polemical context of Carneades' move. Supports the claim contextually rather than naming voluntary self-motion.

quote_evidence: Τὸ αὐτεξούσιον ἐπιδείκνυσι τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
rationale: Irenaeus, Adversus Haereses IV.37.1 (Greek fragments, TLG 1447): the opening of the very chapter the node cites (IV.37), proclaiming human self-determination (autexousion) and God's counseling rather than coercive nature against Gnostic determinism. Supports the node's core claim of Irenaean Selbstbestimmung; the specific reductio of IV.37.6-7 (natura vs voluntas) is not in the corpus — only IV.37.1 is.

quote_evidence: Νοῦς δὲ ὁ ἕνεκά του λογιζόμενος καὶ ὁ πρακτικός· διαφέρει δὲ τοῦ θεωρητικοῦ τῷ τέλει.
rationale: This is De Anima III.10, the exact locus named by the node. The passage states that practical intellect (reasoning for the sake of an end) differs from theoretical intellect by its telos, and continues 'εὐλόγως ταῦτα δύο φαίνεται τὰ κινοῦντα, ὄρεξις καὶ διάνοια πρακτική' — thought and desire as the joint movers of action, precisely the node's claim that practical intellect is oriented toward action and that action issues from the convergence of thought and desire.

quote_evidence: ὅταν δὲ μία γένηται ἐξ αὐτῶν, ἀνάγκη τὸ συμπερανθὲν ἔνθα μὲν φάναι τὴν ψυχήν, ἐν δὲ ταῖς ποιητικαῖς πράττειν εὐθύς
rationale: This is Nicomachean Ethics VII.3, the second locus named by the node — the locus classicus of the practical syllogism: when the universal and particular premises unite, in practical matters the soul must act at once. The passage also contains 'ἀνάγκη τὸν δυνάμενον καὶ μὴ κωλυόμενον ἅμα τοῦτο καὶ πράττειν', matching the node's clause that action issues 'without impediment'.

quote_evidence: καὶ αἱ μὲν μετὰ λόγου πᾶσαι τῶν ἐναντίων αἱ αὐταί, αἱ δὲ ἄλογοι μία ἑνός
rationale: Metaphysics IX.2, the chapter the node summarizes: rational powers (μετὰ λόγου) are all powers of opposites, while non-rational powers are each of one effect only — the passage gives Aristotle's own examples (the hot only heats, medicine produces both disease and health). This is the exact two-way/one-way distinction the node describes.

quote_evidence: ἀνάγκη ἄρα ἕτερόν τι εἶναι τὸ κύριον· λέγω δὲ τοῦτο ὄρεξιν ἢ προαίρεσιν.
rationale: Metaphysics IX.5, explicitly named by the node ('In IX.5 he adds that the exercise of rational powers depends on desire or choice'): since a two-way power cannot produce both opposites at once, something else must be decisive (τὸ κύριον), namely desire or choice (ὄρεξιν ἢ προαίρεσιν). Verbatim support for the node's central claim.

quote_evidence: Ἔτι γὰρ Χριστὸς ὄντων ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν ἔτι κατὰ καιρὸν ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν ἀπέθανεν
rationale: Rom 5:6: Christ died 'for the ungodly' (ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν) while recipients were 'weak' — the primary Pauline locus for Barclay's incongruity thesis: the gift given precisely in the absence of worth.

quote_evidence: ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν
rationale: Rom 5:8: 'while we were still sinners Christ died for us' — explicit statement that the Christ-gift was given without regard to recipients' worth, the core textual evidence for the incongruous gift.

quote_evidence: μήπω γὰρ γεννηθέντων μηδὲ πραξάντων τι ἀγαθὸν ἢ ⸀φαῦλον, ἵνα ἡ κατ’ ἐκλογὴν πρόθεσις τοῦ θεοῦ μένῃ,
rationale: Rom 9:11: election before the twins 'had done anything good or bad' — divine giving in the explicit absence of any prior worth or deed, a key text in Barclay's reading of incongruous grace in Rom 9.

quote_evidence: οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἀλλ’ ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος
rationale: Rom 9:12: 'not from works but from the one who calls' — the call disregards criteria of worth; grounds Barclay's claim that the gift is distributed without regard to worth and itself creates the recipients' standing.

quote_evidence: ⸀θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἐν ὑμῖν καὶ τὸ θέλειν καὶ τὸ ἐνεργεῖν ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας.
rationale: Phil 2:13: God 'works in you both the willing and the working' — the classic non-contrastive agency text: human willing/acting is sourced in, not displaced by, divine agency. Corpus lacks Rom 8:9-14, so this is the most probative available locus for Barclay's claim.

quote_evidence: καθὼς πάντοτε ὑπηκούσατε, μὴ ὡς ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ μου μόνον ἀλλὰ νῦν πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν τῇ ἀπουσίᾳ μου, μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου τὴν ἑαυτῶν σωτηρίαν κατεργάζεσθε,
rationale: Phil 2:12: Paul issues imperatives to believers ('work out your own salvation') — directly evidences the node's point that believers are addressed as real agents, not 'puppets on a string', even as their agency is divinely enabled (v. 13).

quote_evidence: εἰ ζῶμεν πνεύματι, πνεύματι καὶ στοιχῶμεν.
rationale: Gal 5:25: life is given by the Spirit (indicative), yet believers are exhorted to walk by the Spirit (hortatory) — expressing in action what is already created, exactly the asymmetric Spirit-enabled agency the node describes.

quote_evidence: ἔτι κατὰ καιρὸν ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν ἀπέθανεν
rationale: Rom 5:6: the gift given 'for the ungodly' — the 'unconditioned' pole of Barclay's distinction (no prior merit or worth required). Corpus lacks Rom 4:5 and Rom 2:6-16, so this is the strongest available Romans locus.

quote_evidence: καὶ τοῦτο οὐκ ἐξ ὑμῶν, θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον·
rationale: Eph 2:8: salvation is 'the gift of God, not from yourselves' — explicit Pauline statement of the gift's unconditioned character (no prior conditions in the recipient).

quote_evidence: κτισθέντες ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ἐπὶ ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς οἷς προητοίμασεν ὁ θεὸς ἵνα ἐν αὐτοῖς περιπατήσωμεν.
rationale: Eph 2:10: recipients are 'created in Christ Jesus for good works' — the gift is unconditioned (2:8-9) yet not unconditional: it is designed to produce doers of the good, precisely the 'free but not cheap' structure of the node.

quote_evidence: ἵνα κομίσηται ἕκαστος τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος πρὸς ἃ ἔπραξεν, εἴτε ἀγαθὸν εἴτε ⸀φαῦλον.
rationale: 2 Cor 5:10: each receives 'according to what he has done, whether good or bad' — the judgment-according-to-works pole whose apparent tension with justification of the ungodly the node claims Barclay's distinction resolves.

quote_evidence: καὶ ἡ χάρις αὐτοῦ ἡ εἰς ἐμὲ οὐ κενὴ ἐγενήθη, ἀλλὰ περισσότερον αὐτῶν πάντων ἐκοπίασα, οὐκ ἐγὼ δὲ ἀλλὰ ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ ⸀ἡ σὺν ἐμοί.
rationale: 1 Cor 15:10: grace 'was not in vain' but issued in Paul's labor — 'not I but the grace of God with me'. The paradigmatic text for grace that is circular only by remaking the agent who responds, and 'ineffective and unfulfilled' without that response.

quote_evidence: θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἐν ὑμῖν καὶ τὸ θέλειν καὶ τὸ ἐνεργεῖν
rationale: Phil 2:13: God energizes the believers' willing and working — the 'newly competent agents' whose obedient practice is integral to (not instrumental toward) the one gift. Rom 6:15-23 (slavery to Righteousness) is absent from the corpus; this is the closest available locus.

quote_evidence: καθὼς πάντοτε ὑπηκούσατε
rationale: Phil 2:12: 'as you have always obeyed' followed by the command to work out salvation — the obliging, obedience-expecting character of the gift expressed in the recipients' bodily practice.

quote_evidence: ἔστω δὲ πρὸς τὸ σαφὲς τῶν περὶ ἡμᾶς νῦν ὄντων, ὅτι οὐ συμβαίνει ἀπὸ τῶν οὐρανίων, ὡς πάντων αἰτιῶν ὄντων, καὶ τὸ ἐμὲ γράφειν νυνὶ τάδε καὶ ὡδὶ σέ τε πράττειν ἅπερ καὶ ὅπως τυγχάνεις πράττων· πάλιν τοίνυν ἐπειδὰν ἡ αὐτὴ ἀφίκηται αἰτία, ταὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως οἱ αὐτοὶ γενόμενοι πράξομεν
rationale: This is the exact locus the node names (ps.-Plutarch, On Fate 569, ch. 3). It states the doctrine Boys-Stones reconstructs: exact cyclical recurrence tied to the cosmic period ('when the same cause arrives, we, become the same persons, will do the same things in the same way' — including the author writing this very treatise again), while explicitly denying that the heavenly bodies are the causes of everything ('οὐ συμβαίνει ἀπὸ τῶν οὐρανίων, ὡς πάντων αἰτιῶν ὄντων'), i.e. recurrence is causal but not astral determinism.

quote_evidence: Ἀνάγκη τοίνυν κατὰ τοῦτον τὸν λόγον τῶν ἀστέρων ἐκ μακρᾶς περιόδου ἐλθόντων ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτὴν σχέσιν πρὸς ἀλλήλους, ὁποίαν εἶχον ἐπὶ Σωκράτους, πάλιν Σωκράτη γενέσθαι ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν καὶ τὰ αὐτὰ παθεῖν, κατηγορούμενον ὑπὸ Ἀνύτου καὶ Μελήτου
rationale: This passage IS Origen, Contra Celsum 5.21 (SC 147, ch. 21 = §29 in this corpus segmentation), the second locus the node explicitly cites. Origen reports that the Pythagoreans and Platonists ('οἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ Πυθαγόρου δὲ καὶ Πλάτωνος'), while keeping the cosmos indestructible, hold that when the stars return to the same configuration over a long period, Socrates is born again from the same parents and suffers the same things, accused by Anytus and Meletus — the testimonium for Platonist exact cyclical recurrence Boys-Stones uses.

quote_evidence: πάλιν τοίνυν ἐπειδὰν ἡ αὐτὴ ἀφίκηται αἰτία, ταὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως οἱ αὐτοὶ γενόμενοι πράξομεν. οὕτω δὲ καὶ πάντες ἄνθρωποι καὶ τὰ γʼ ἑξῆς κατὰ τὴν ἑξῆς αἰτίαν γενήσεται καὶ πραχθήσεται
rationale: Primary Platonist evidence for the first leg of Boys-Stones's argument: ps.-Plutarch, De fato 3 (569) accepts full causal determination of individual embodied actions ('when the same cause arrives, the same persons will do and undergo the same things; so too all men, each thing happening according to its successive cause') — choices are causally inevitable yet remain the agents' own. Boys-Stones's framing (autonomy = independence from external agency, the runs-into vs pushed example) is his own modern construct, so confidence stays in the discussion band.

quote_evidence: ἵνα τοῖς ἔπειτα εἴη κακίας ἑκάστων ἀναίτιος
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch, De fato 9 (572f-574): the hierarchy of three providences. The first god orders things only 'μέχρι ψυχῶν ἀνθρωπίνων' and legislates fate precisely so that he 'be blameless of the vice of each individual' (Timaeus 42d quoted), delegating particulars to younger gods and daimones, and the mortal creature becomes 'cause of evils to itself' (ὅ τι μὴ κακῶν αὐτὸ αὑτῷ γίγνοιτο αἴτιον). This is the Platonist move Boys-Stones describes: removing individuals from the supreme god's direct remit is what leaves their choices their own — no external agent owns them.

quote_evidence: Λέγεται οὖν τὸ μὲν ἁπλῶς θέλειν θέλησις ἤτοι ἡ θελητικὴ δύναμις λογικὴ οὖσα ὄρεξις καὶ θέλημα φυσικόν· τὸ δὲ πῶς θέλειν ἤτοι τὸ τῇ θελήσει ὑποκείμενον θελητὸν καὶ θέλημα γνωμικόν
rationale: John of Damascus, Expositio fidei 58 (III.14) transmits the Maximian natural/gnomic will distinction near-verbatim from Maximus's Opuscula: the simple capacity to will is θέλημα φυσικόν (a rational appetitive faculty), the determinate 'how one wills' is θέλημα γνωμικόν. This is the very distinction the node attributes to Maximus via Blowers pp. 121-123. Testimonium because Maximus's own Opusculum 1 and Disputatio cum Pyrrho (PG 91), Blowers's actual texts, are not in the corpus; the Damascene is the canonical early witness to the doctrine.

quote_evidence: Διὸ οὐδὲ γνωμικὸν εἶχε θέλημα. Θέλησιν μὲν γὰρ εἶχε τὴν φυσικὴν, τὴν ἁπλῆν, τὴν ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ὑποστάσεσι τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὁμοίως θεωρουμένην
rationale: Expositio fidei 36 (II.22) applies the same Maximian distinction: Christ had the natural, simple θέλησις seen alike in all human hypostases, but no gnomic will, since γνώμη 'συνδιαιρεῖται ταῖς ὑποστάσεσι' — gnome varies with the individual hypostasis, exactly the deliberative-elective experiential will of fallen agents that Blowers reconstructs as needing training. Indirect witness (Damascene, not Maximus's own text).

quote_evidence: θελητικὸν δέ ἐστι τὸ πεφυκὸς θέλειν, οἷον θελητική ἐστιν ἡ θεία φύσις, ὡσαύτως καὶ ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη
rationale: Expositio fidei 58 states the core doctrinal claim of the node in the Maximian tradition: θέλησις is 'ἡ θελητικὴ δύναμις λογικὴ οὖσα ὄρεξις' — a faculty (δύναμις) of rational appetite — and what is volitional is 'that which by nature wills' (τὸ πεφυκὸς θέλειν), a property of φύσις (divine and human alike), not of the hypostasis. This is the will-as-natural-appetitive-faculty conception (parallel to the Clement-derived δύναμις τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ὄντος ὀρεκτική) that Blowers pp. 159-161 attributes to Maximus. Testimonium via the Damascene; the Nemesius-based process reconstruction itself (Opusc. 1 + Disp. Pyrrho) is not directly groundable here.

quote_evidence: τὸ δὲ πῶς θέλειν ἤτοι τὸ τῇ θελήσει ὑποκείμενον θελητὸν καὶ θέλημα γνωμικόν
rationale: Expositio fidei 58 contains the node's key technical phrase verbatim: τὸ πῶς θέλειν ('the how of willing') is distinguished from the simple θέλειν of nature and relocated to the gnomic order, while 'φυσικὰ γὰρ καὶ οὐχ ὑποστατικά φαμεν τὰ θελήματα' keeps the wills themselves on the side of nature. This is precisely the wills-vs-mode-of-willing distinction Blowers (pp. 52, 164) identifies as the hinge of Maximus's mature Christology, transmitted by the Damascene from Maximus's Opuscula (which are themselves absent from the corpus).

quote_evidence: Διὸ οὐδὲ γνωμικὸν εἶχε θέλημα. Θέλησιν μὲν γὰρ εἶχε τὴν φυσικὴν, τὴν ἁπλῆν
rationale: Expositio fidei 36 gives the Christological payoff the node describes: because γνώμη belongs to the hypostatic mode rather than to nature, Christ possesses the complete natural human θέλησις yet has no gnomic will — denying γνώμη in Christ without denying his human natural will, exactly the solution Blowers attributes to Maximus's logos-tropos distinction. Indirect (Damascene) witness.

quote_evidence: τὸ δʼ ἐφʼ ἡμῖν ὡς κύριον χρῆσθαι τῷ ἐνδεχομένῳ
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 6 (570e-571a) is the central Middle Platonist text exhibiting τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν as a technical category of agent-control (the agent as 'master' using the contingent), not 'freedom of the will' — exactly the usage Boys-Stones says is prejudicially translated. Grounds the primary-text basis of the terminological claim; the scholarly layer (Eliasson, Frede vs Dihle) is modern and not itself groundable in ancient passages.

quote_evidence: ἥ τε προαίρεσις καὶ τὸ ἐφʼ ἡμῖν, ἥ τε τύχη καὶ τὸ αὐτόματον
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 8 (574b) lists τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν alongside προαίρεσις, chance and the spontaneous as categories contained within fate but not occurring according to fate — showing the Middle Platonist eph' hēmin as agent-autonomy within a causal framework, supporting Boys-Stones' warning against retrojecting libertarian 'free will' onto it.

quote_evidence: οἷος ὁ πολιτικὸς νόμος ὃς πρῶτον μὲν τὰ πλεῖστα, εἰ καὶ μὴ πάντα, ἐξ ὑποθέσεως προστάττει
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 4 (569d-570a) is the very text Boys-Stones interprets: fate is like the civic law that 'commands ex hypothesi', covering things universally (τὰ μὲν καθόλου προηγουμένως) and explicitly NOT operating at the individual level (πλὴν οὐχ ἥ γε κατὰ μέρος οὐδʼ ἡ καθʼ ἕκαστα, same passage). Direct primary anchor of the 'hypothetical fate' doctrine; the node names ps.-Plutarch.

quote_evidence: ἃ δὴ πάντα περιέχει μὲν ἡ εἱμαρμένη, οὐδὲν δʼ αὐτῶν ἐστι καθʼ εἱμαρμένην
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 8 (574b): fate contains everything (the contingent, choice, what is up to us, chance) yet none of these is according to fate — the precise textual basis for 'everything hypothetically fated but nothing fated absolutely'.

quote_evidence: ἡ δὲ κατʼ οὐσίαν ἔοικεν εἶναι σύμπασʼ ἡ τοῦ κόσμου ψυχὴ τριχῇ διανεμηθεῖσα
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 2 (568e): fate 'as substance' is the whole world soul in its threefold division — the node's claim that 'fate as substance is identified with the world soul' paraphrases this passage directly.

quote_evidence: εἱμαρμένη διχῶς καὶ λέγεται καὶ νοεῖται· ἡ μὲν γάρ ἐστιν ἐνέργεια ἡ δʼ οὐσία
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 1 (568c-d): the opening distinction between fate as activity (the divine law Plato states in Phaedrus/Timaeus/Republic) and fate as substance — the framework underlying the node's 'fate as activity is those laws playing out at the individual level'. NB: the parallel Alcinous Didaskalikos 26 is not yet in the corpus.

quote_evidence: οὐχ ὑμᾶς δαίμων λήξεται, ἀλλ' ὑμεῖς δαίμονα αἱρήσεσθε. πρῶτος δ' ὁ λαχὼν πρῶτος αἱρείσθω βίον ᾧ συνέσται ἐξ ἀνάγκης
rationale: Republic 10.617d-e, the prophet's proclamation in the Myth of Er — the locus the node names (source K): the discarnate soul itself chooses its daimon/life, with no compulsion as to which (and αἰτία ἑλομένου· θεὸς ἀναίτιος follows in the same passage), while the chosen life will then attach ἐξ ἀνάγκης — exactly the prima facie evidence for discarnate indeterminacy combined with embodied determination that Boys-Stones discusses.

quote_evidence: κατὰ συνήθειαν γὰρ τοῦ προτέρου βίου τὰ πολλὰ αἱρεῖσθαι
rationale: Republic 10.620a: most souls choose 'according to the habit of their former life' — the textual counter-evidence that the discarnate choice may itself be character-determined, which is integral to Boys-Stones' own doubt that any Platonist intended genuine indeterminacy (DCD3).

quote_evidence: οὐ γὰρ ἑαυτὸν αἰτιᾶσθαι τῶν κακῶν, ἀλλὰ τύχην τε καὶ δαίμονας καὶ πάντα μᾶλλον ἀνθʼ ἑαυτοῦ
rationale: Republic 10.619b-c: the first-lot soul rashly chooses tyranny and then blames fortune and daimones rather than himself — responsibility lodged in the discarnate soul's own choice, part of the Myth-of-Er dossier the node interprets.

quote_evidence: ἀπείρων γὰρ ἐξ ἀπείρου καὶ εἰς ἄπειρον ὄντων τῶν γιγνομένων, τὰ πάντα περιβαλοῦσʼ ἐν κύκλῳ ἡ εἱμαρμένη οὐκ ἄπειρος; ἀλλὰ πεπερασμένη ἐστίν οὔτε γὰρ νόμος οὔτε λόγος οὔτε τι θεῖον ἄπειρον ἂν εἴη
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 3 (569a): events are infinite from infinity to infinity, but fate — being law, logos, something divine — is finite. The primary-text basis for Boys-Stones' premise that the infinitely many individuals of an everlasting cosmos exceed what any divine planning can determine.

quote_evidence: πλὴν οὐχ ἥ γε κατὰ μέρος οὐδʼ ἡ καθʼ ἕκαστα
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 4 (569d): fate is expressly NOT fate of the part or of individuals; like civic law it provides for things universally (καθόλου προηγουμένως) with individual cases falling under it only consequentially — the structural claim that divine causation operates at the species/universal level, never determining individuals.

quote_evidence: ἡ δὲ δευτέρα δευτέρων θεῶν τῶν κατʼ οὐρανὸν ἰόντων, καθʼ ἣν τά τε θνητὰ γίγνεται τεταγμένως καὶ ὅσα πρὸς διαμονὴν καὶ σωτηρίαν ἑκάστων τῶν γενῶν
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 9 (572f-573a): the second providence (heavenly gods) ensures the orderly generation of mortals and the preservation and continuance of each of the GENERA — providence cares that the kinds/species exist, not which individuals do, exactly the doctrine Boys-Stones reconstructs.

quote_evidence: Καὶ οἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ Πυθαγόρου δὲ καὶ Πλάτωνος εἰ καὶ δοκοῦσιν ἄφθαρτον τηρεῖν τὸν κόσμον, ἀλλὰ τοῖς παραπλη-σίοις γε περιπίπτουσι
rationale: This SC 147 passage IS Contra Celsum 5.21, the exact locus the node names (source I): Pythagoreans and Platonists, despite keeping the cosmos indestructible, 'fall into the same difficulties' as the Stoics — astral periodic recurrence entails Socrates accused again by Anytus and Meletus. Origen then contrasts the Christian view of God governing τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν ἑκάστου in the same passage. Directly evidences 'Platonists do no better than Stoics'. The further loci De Principiis 1.8.1 and 3.5.2 are NOT in the corpus (only De Princ III.1 and IV extracts are ingested).

quote_evidence: ἔστιν οὖν πρόνοια ἡ μὲν ἀνωτάτω καὶ πρώτη τοῦ πρώτου θεοῦ νόησις, εἴτε καὶ βούλησις οὖσα εὐεργέτις ἁπάντων, καθʼ ἣν πρώτως ἕκαστα τῶν θείων διὰ παντὸς ἄριστά τε καὶ κάλλιστα κεκόσμηται. ἡ δὲ δευτέρα δευτέρων θεῶν τῶν κατʼ οὐρανὸν ἰόντων
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 9 (572F-573A) is a principal source in Boys-Stones 2018 ch. 11 for the Platonist three-tier providence scheme the node reconstructs: highest/first providence as the intellection-volition of the first god, secondary providence exercised by the secondary (heavenly) gods. This Greek passage (work urn_cts_greeklit_tlg0007_tlg108_grc) is the locus classicus of the doctrine of providence 'by proxy'.

quote_evidence: τὸ μὲν συλλαμβάνειν τισὶ τὸ δαιμόνιον κατὰ τὴν τρίτην πρόνοιαν ἀναθετέον
rationale: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 10 (Greek) explicitly assigns the daimonion's assistance of certain humans to the THIRD providence — the precise ancient warrant for the node's claim that daimons exercise 'tertiary providence' continuous with divine care over human ethical life. Same chapter also relates second providence to fate, matching the node's by-proxy transmission scheme.

quote_evidence: Since providence is triple: the first, having generated fate, in a way encompasses it; the second, co-generated with fate, is wholly encompassed by it; the third, having come to be after fate, is likewise contained within it
rationale: English version of Ps.-Plutarch De fato 17 (work urn_cts_greeklit_tlg0007_tlg099_eng) states the triple-providence hierarchy and continues 'the daimonion assisting some must be referred to the third providence' — directly evidencing the secondary/tertiary providence-by-proxy structure that Boys-Stones reconstructs (his Source A). quote_evidence: ἧς ἐπιμελούμενος καὶ ἐν ᾗ τὰ σαυτοῦ τιθέμενος οὐδέποτε κωλυθήσῃ - caring for this and placing your own things in it, you will never be hindered
rationale: Diss. 1.1 (Zeus speech): even Zeus could not make body and possessions free; freedom lies solely in the inner faculty of using impressions — evidencing Long's claim that Epictetan freedom is freedom from constraint by externals, internal and ethical, not freedom from antecedent causation.

quote_evidence: τῷ συγκαταθετικῷ τόπῳ ἀκώλυτος εἶ καὶ ἀνεμπόδιστος - in the sphere of ASSENT you are unhindered and unimpeded
rationale: Diss. 4.1.69-83 (the discourse On Freedom, central to Long's section 8.3): only assent and impulse are unhindered while bodily execution can be blocked — freedom as internal autonomy within the causal order, not exemption from it.

quote_evidence: a human being, having nothing more authoritative than prohairesis, but with other things subject to it, unenslaved and unhindered
rationale: Diss. 2.10.1 (in passage Diss. 2.9.18-2.10.8) is the locus classicus Long uses to show prohairesis functioning as Epictetus's supreme technical term — 'nothing more authoritative (kyrioteron) than prohairesis' assigns to prohairesis the role earlier Stoics gave the hegemonikon. The comparative claim ('only Stoic') is Long's lexical observation and cannot be evidenced by a single passage, hence not higher confidence.

quote_evidence: Do you see that in this respect you have your prohairesis unhindered, unforced, unimpeded?
rationale: Diss. 1.17.21-28 (in passage Diss. 1.17.12-27), a chapter Long cites, shows prohairesis as a fully developed technical term in Epictetus ('unhindered by nature and unforced'), evidencing the claim that he made it central to his philosophy.

quote_evidence: a human being, having nothing more authoritative than prohairesis, but with other things subject to it, unenslaved and unhindered
rationale: Diss. 2.10.1 directly evidences Long's claim that prohairesis names the purposive centre of a person: a human being is defined as the one for whom prohairesis is supreme and everything else subject to it.

quote_evidence: Of the other faculties, you will find none that contemplates itself
rationale: Diss. 1.1.3-19 is the passage Long glosses as the 'reasoning, self-studying faculty that God has given each person': only the rational faculty contemplates itself, and Zeus says 'I gave you a part of our own'. This grounds the 'self-conscious centre' and God-given 'me' components of Long's claim (the word prohairesis itself does not appear in this stretch, hence 0.75).

quote_evidence: My prohairesis you will not bind
rationale: Diss. 1.1.23 (in passage Diss. 1.1.19-1.2.8): the tyrant can bind the leg but not prohairesis — exactly Long's point that the essence of the self lies not in externally impedible bodily action but in the mental dispositions behind it.

quote_evidence: ὑποσημαίνειν δʼ ἔοικε καὶ τοὔνομα ὡς ὂν πρὸ ἑτέρων αἱρετόν
rationale: Aristotle, EN III.2 1112a16-17: the very passage behind Long's etymological gloss of prohairesis as 'pre-choice/choice before choice' — the name 'seems to hint that it is what is chosen before (pro) other things', and prohairesis is 'meta logou kai dianoias' (with reason and thought), i.e. the deliberative mental process preceding action.

quote_evidence: Socrates was perfected in this way, attending to nothing else in all that was presented to him than to reason. But you, even if you are not yet, you ought to live as one who wishes to be Socrates.
rationale: Ench. 51.3 is the classic locus for Long's thesis that Socrates, not any Stoic predecessor, is Epictetus's authorizing life-model: the pupil is told to live 'as one who wishes to be Socrates'. The same passage (Ench. 53) closes with Socrates' words from Plato's Apology ('Anytus and Meletus can kill me, but not harm me').

quote_evidence: After Socrates died, his memory is no less, or even more, useful to people than what he did while still alive. These are the doctrines. Look to these examples
rationale: Diss. 4.1.159-169 (in passage Diss. 4.1.160-176): in the climactic discourse On Freedom, Epictetus holds up Socrates — not Zeno or Chrysippus — as THE exemplar to look to ('Look to these examples'), supporting Long's claim that Socrates is the primary authorizing paradigm of the Discourses.

quote_evidence: ἐφ' ἡμῖν μὲν ὑπόληψις, ὁρμή, ὄρεξις, ἔκκλισις, καὶ ἑνὶ λόγῳ ὅσα ἡμέτερα ἔργα· οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν δὲ τὸ σῶμα
rationale: The canonical Epictetan statement of the eph' hēmin doctrine that Long's framing rests on: only judgement (hypolēpsis), impulse, desire and aversion — our own mental acts — are up to us, while the body and externals are not. This is precisely the doctrine Long identifies as Epictetus's principal project.

quote_evidence: τὸ κράτιστον ἁπάντων καὶ κυριεῦον οἱ θεοὶ μόνον ἐφʼ ἡμῖν ἐποίησαν, τὴν χρῆσιν τὴν ὀρθὴν ταῖς φαντασίαις
rationale: Discourses 1.1.7-12 (full Greek in corpus): the gods made only the right use of impressions up to us; Zeus's speech adds that even the body is 'not yours, but cleverly kneaded clay' (1.1.11) and that caring for what is ours means 'you will never be hindered, never impeded' (1.1.12) — exactly Long's corollary that nothing external can constrain us unless we permit it.

quote_evidence: Ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ ἀργὸς καλούμενος λόγος, σόφισμα ὤν, τοιοῦτός ἐστι
rationale: SVF II.957 preserves verbatim the Greek of Contra Celsum II.20 — the exact locus the node names for Origen's rebuttal of the Idle/Lazy Argument: Origen calls 'the so-called idle argument' a sophism and refutes it with the sick-man/doctor and Laius examples.

quote_evidence: Περὶ αὐτεξουσίου, καὶ τῶν δοκούντων τοῦτο ἀναιρεῖνῥητῶν γραφικῶν λύσις καὶ ἑρμηνεία
rationale: SC 268 Greek text of De Principiis III.1: the chapter heading literally opens 'Peri autexousiou' (On free choice), exactly as the node claims — Origen's most systematic defense of moral freedom.

quote_evidence: Du destin. Comment notre liberté est sauvegardée alors que Dieu connaît à l'avance les actes de chacun. Comment les astres ne sont pas les agents des événements humains, mais seulement les signes.
rationale: Titulus of Philocalia 23 (SC 226), the very chapter the node cites: Origen's polemic against astral/heimarmenē determinism, explicitly an extract from book III of his Commentary on Genesis — stars are signs, not causes, and human freedom is preserved despite divine foreknowledge.

quote_evidence: qu'il existe des naturesd'âmes telles que de toute façon elles périssent ou sontsauvées
rationale: De Principiis III.1.8: Origen states the 'heretics' (gnostic) doctrine of fixed natures of souls — saved or lost by nature, incapable of change — which he then refutes at length; this is the anti-gnostic 'natures' polemic the node describes as destroying autexousion.

quote_evidence: οὐδενὸς ἄλλου ἔργον ἐστὶν ἢ τοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν λόγου, τουτέστι τῆς αὐτεξουσίου ἡμῶν κρίσεως
rationale: De Principiis III.1.3 (= Philocalia 21.3, SC 226 Junod): Origen identifies to autexousion with the judging activity of the reason (logos) within us — 'our self-determining judgment' — not with any separate faculty of will. Primary-text testimonium for Sytsma's anti-anachronism point that the rational mind is the subject of choice.

quote_evidence: τὸ δὲ κρῖναι οὑτωσὶ χρήσασθαι τῷ γενομένῳ ἢ ἑτέρως,οὐκ ἄλλου τινὸς ἔργον ἢ τοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν λόγου ἐστίν
rationale: SC 268 Greek of De Principiis III.1.3: judging how to use what befalls us 'is the work of nothing other than the reason in us' — choice is an act of logos judging impressions (κρίνοντα τὰς φαντασίας), with no independent will-faculty in the picture, as Sytsma argues.

quote_evidence: φέρε καὶ τὰ περὶ τοῦ αὐτεξουσίου ἰδίᾳ ὀλίγα διαλάβωμεν
rationale: De Principiis III.1.1: under the heading 'Περὶ αὐτεξουσίου' Origen announces a dedicated technical treatment of to autexousion as 'a most necessary problem', in the same sentence using the older technical phrase τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν ('τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν εἶναι τὰ ἐπαίνου καὶ ψόγου ἄξια') — attesting both technical terms Sytsma identifies, and Origen's insistence on unfolding the concept's precise ἔννοια.

quote_evidence: τὸ δὲ ὁρίσαι καὶ δοκιμάσαι πῶς τούτοις χρηστέον... οὐδενὸς ἄλλου ἔργον ἐστὶν ἢ τοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν λόγου, τουτέστι τῆς αὐτεξουσίου ἡμῶν κρίσεως
rationale: De Principiis III.1.3 (Philocalia 21.3): Origen's technical definition deploying both terms together — what is not eph' hēmin (externals) versus τῆς αὐτεξουσίου ἡμῶν κρίσεως — showing autexousion functioning as a precise term for moral autonomy/rational self-determination, not a vague 'free will'.

quote_evidence: Il est possible qu'il fasse ceci, mais aussi le contraire ; or, bien que les deux soient possibles, je sais qu'il fera ceci.
rationale: Philocalia 23.9 (Origen, Comm. on Genesis III apud Philoc.; SC 226 French translation, corpus work_origen_philocalia_grc). The Judas/Peter analysis is the primary locus behind Sytsma's hinge: God knows in advance which of two genuinely open possibilities the soul will freely realize ('bien que les deux soient possibles, je sais qu'il fera ceci'), so the outcome is guaranteed to God while binary alternatives in the moment are preserved.

quote_evidence: les multiples événements qui ne dépen- dent pas de nous soient les causes de nombreux événements qui dépendent de nous
rationale: Philocalia 23.11: Origen explicitly concedes that external events not up to us are causes of many acts that ARE up to us — i.e. external circumstances condition (without necessitating) free responses, since 'il est possible qu'à la suite des mêmes événements antérieurs il se produise autre chose'. This is precisely the circumstance-arranging mechanism Sytsma attributes to Origen's God.

quote_evidence: λογικὸν ζῷον καὶ λόγον ἔχει πρὸς τῇφανταστικῇ φύσει, τὸν κρίνοντα τὰς φαντασίας καὶ τινὰςμὲν ἀποδοκιμάζοντα τινὰς δὲ παραδεχόμενον
rationale: De Principiis III.1.2-3 (SC 268 Greek, whole chapter Περὶ αὐτεξουσίου in one corpus passage). This is the exact locus of Sytsma's claim: Origen deploys the Stoic mechanics of choice — 'φαντασίας ἐγγινομένης ὁρμὴν προκαλουμένης' (impression provoking impulse, with spider/bee examples), and the rational animal's logos judging impressions, rejecting some and accepting others. Origen visibly adopting the phantasia–assent–hormē psychology.

quote_evidence: Τὰ μὲν ἔξωθεν ἡμῖν συμβαίνοντα οὐκ ἔστιν ἐφ' ἡμῖν· τὸ δὲ ὁρίσαι καὶ δοκιμάσαι πῶς τούτοις χρηστέον... οὐδενὸς ἄλλου ἔργον ἐστὶν ἢ τοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν λόγου, τουτέστι τῆς αὐτεξουσίου ἡμῶν κρίσεως
rationale: De Principiis III.1.3 (Greek verified Philocalia 21.3, SC 226 Junod): externals are not eph' hēmin, but judging how to use them is the work of the self-determining krisis — the Epictetan-flavoured distinction that supports Sytsma's placing of Origen between Epictetus and Alexander of Aphrodisias on assent and 'what is up to us'.

quote_evidence: ἡμεῖς δὲ τῆς λογικῆς φύσεώς φαμεν ὅλης κρατῆσαί ποτε τὸν λόγον καὶ μεταποιῆσαι πᾶσαν ψυχὴν εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ τελειότητα, ἐπὰν ἕκαστος ψιλῇ χρησάμενος τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ ἕληται ἃ βούλεται
rationale: Contra Celsum VIII.72 (corpus canonical_ref mislabeled '1.72' in sc_origenes_contra_celsum_grc — text is the Book VIII.72 reply to Celsus's 'one law' prayer). The classic universalist assertion in Origen's own voice: the Logos will one day master the WHOLE rational nature and transform EVERY soul into his own perfection — through each one's free exercise of exousia. The passage even ends with the guarded deferral 'πότερον δὲ ὥστε μηδαμῇ μηδαμῶς ἔτι αὐτὴν ἐπιτραπῆναι δύνασθαι ἢ μή, οὐ τοῦ παρόντος ἐστὶ λόγου διδάξαι', exactly the 'deliberately guarded statements' on permanence that Sytsma's argument addresses.

quote_evidence: Dieu, lorsqu'il s'est mis à penser au commencement de la création du monde - comme rien n'arrive sans cause -, a parcouru de son intelligence chacun des futurs
rationale: Philocalia 23.8 (Comm. on Genesis III; SC 226 translation): at the moment of creation God mentally traversed the entire causal chain of futures to the end ('il a vu que, quand telle chose arrive, telle autre suit... jusqu'à la fin des choses') without thereby causing them. This is the Origenian prearrangement-at-creation basis on which Sytsma builds his preselection thesis.

quote_evidence: οὐχ ὅτι γινώσκει ὁ θεὸς τὸ ἐσόμενον, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἔσται· ἀλλ' ὅτι ἐσόμενόν ἐστι, διὰ τοῦτο γινώσκεται ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι
rationale: De Oratione 6 (GCS 3 Koetschau): God's prescience is not the cause of what will be — it is because it will be that God foreknows it. This non-causal foreknowledge is the component by which Sytsma's God foreordains the outcome THROUGH rather than against free choices, never coercing the moment of choice ('escaping the charge of fatalism').

quote_evidence: Οὐκοῦν ἐγκαταλείπεται θείᾳ κρίσει ὀ ἐγκατα-λειπόμενος καὶ μακροθυμεῖ ἐπί τινας τῶν ἁμαρτανόντωνὁ θεὸς οὐκ ἀλόγως, ἀλλ' ὡς αὐτοῖς συνοίσοντος ὡς πρὸςτὴν ἀθανασίαν τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ τὸν ἄπειρον αἰῶνα τοῦ μὴταχὺ συνεργηθῆναι εἰς σωτηρίαν
rationale: De Principiis III.1.13 (within the SC 268 Greek chapter passage): even divine ABANDONMENT is judged providence aimed at the abandoned soul's own benefit 'with regard to the soul's immortality and the unending age' — salvation reached more securely after experiencing evils, with the physician analogy (ἰατροί delaying cure to heal more safely) and Pharaoh hardened 'ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ τῶν πολλῶν'. Direct primary evidence for Sytsma's claim (after Drewery/Koch) that every providential act, including punishment and abandonment, is salvific grace.

quote_evidence: Dieu, qui ordonne toutes choses dans le monde d'une manière profitable, a eu raison de nous rendre aveugles aussi devant l'avenir
rationale: Philocalia 23.10 (SC 226 translation): God 'orders all things in the world in a profitable manner' — even hiding the future from us is a providential-pedagogical act serving our becoming good (Koch's pronoia/paideusis theme that Sytsma cites). Clear, though more general, support for providence as wholly beneficent and salvific.

quote_evidence: sed malum sit aversio eius ab incommutabili bono, et conversio ad mutabilia bona: quae tamen aversio atque conversio, quoniam non cogitur, sed est voluntaria, digna et iusta eam miseriae poena subsequitur
rationale: De Libero Arbitrio 2.19.53 — the exact locus named by the node. Contains verbatim the aversio/conversio formula the node quotes ('aversio eius ab incommutabili bono et conversio ad mutabilia bona') plus the voluntariness ('non cogitur, sed est voluntaria') and just-punishment claims.

quote_evidence: Qui tamen defectus quoniam est voluntarius, in nostra est positus potestate
rationale: De Libero Arbitrio 2.20.54 — second locus named by the node ('Defectus iste voluntarius est'). The passage defines the motus aversionis as a defectivus motus ex nihilo, not from God, and states the defectus is voluntary and in our power — exactly the node's claim.

quote_evidence: unde ille motus existat, quo ipsa voluntas avertitur a communi atque incommutabili bono, et ad propria vel aliena vel infima, atque omnia commutabilia convertitur bona
rationale: De Libero Arbitrio 3.1.1 — third locus named by the node. Evodius poses the question of the origin of the aversio-motion and Augustine establishes against natura/necessitas that the movement is culpable only if voluntary, the emphasis on voluntariness the node attributes to this locus.

quote_evidence: οὐχ ὅτι γινώσκει ὁ θεὸς τὸ ἐσόμενον, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἔσται· ἀλλ' ὅτι ἐσόμενόν ἐστι, διὰ τοῦτο γινώσκεται ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι.
rationale: Origen, De Oratione 6 (GCS 3): the primary text for type (1), simple non-causal foreknowledge of what WILL happen — prognosis is not the cause of future events arising from our self-determining motion. This is the textual basis from which Sytsma's typology is reconstructed.

quote_evidence: Si Judas est un traître, Dieu, grâce à sa prescience des deux possibilités mentionnées - étant donné que seule l'une des possibilités peut se réaliser - saura d'avance que Judas sera un traître, car il sait d'avance la vérité. Mais l'événement sur lequel porte la connaissance peut aussi se produire de l'autre façon.
rationale: Philocalia 23.9 (= Comm. Gen. III): the clearest Origenian text for type (2), foreknowledge of future possibilities — God foreknows BOTH possibilities (Judas apostle like Peter / Judas traitor) while knowing which will be realized. Directly evidences the doctrinal material Sytsma reconstructs.

quote_evidence: il a vu que, quand telle chose arrive, telle autre suit, et que quand cette consé- quence s'est produite, telle autre chose s'ensuivra, et que quand celle-ci aura eu lieu, cette autre arrivera. En s'avançant ainsi jusqu'à la fin des choses, il a su ce qui sera, sans être forcément la cause de la réalisation de chacun des événements qu'il connaît.
rationale: Philocalia 23.8: God at creation runs through conditional chains (if X happens, Y follows...) for each free agent, knowing 'quel genre d'homme sera chacun'. This conditional/hypothetical survey of free conduct is the textual basis for Sytsma's reconstructed type (3), counterfactual knowledge of creaturely freedom, which the node itself says Origen never labels as a third type.

quote_evidence: Τὰ μὲν ἔξωθεν ἡμῖν συμβαίνοντα οὐκ ἔστιν ἐφ' ἡμῖν· τὸ δὲ ὁρίσαι καὶ δοκιμάσαι πῶς τούτοις χρηστέον... οὐδενὸς ἄλλου ἔργον ἐστὶν ἢ τοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν λόγου, τουτέστι τῆς αὐτεξουσίου ἡμῶν κρίσεως
rationale: De Principiis III.1.3 (Greek via Philocalia 21, SC 226 Junod): Origen's technical definition — judging and determining how to use externals is the work of nothing other than the reason WITHIN us, our self-determining krisis. This is the textual basis for Sytsma's condition (1), self-origination of assent by the soul itself, not an external agent.

quote_evidence: αἱρούμεθαμὲν τὸ καλὸν ἐκκλίνομεν δὲ τὸ αἰσχρόν, ἐπαινετοὶ μένἐσμεν ἐπιδόντες ἑαυτοὺς τῇ πράξει τοῦ καλοῦ, ψεκτοὶ δὲκατὰ τὸ ἐναντίον
rationale: De Principiis III.1.1-3 Greek (SC 268): the rational animal's logos judges impressions, accepting some and rejecting others, with the two-way capacity to choose the noble or incline to the shameful, grounding praise and blame. Textual basis for Sytsma's condition (2), binary alternative possibilities toward/away from the good.

quote_evidence: Car l'homme n'a absolument pas la faculté de s'envoler, tandis qu'il a la faculté d'être vertueux ou licencieux.
rationale: Philocalia 23.9: Origen explicitly limits two-sided possibility to the moral domain (man cannot fly, but has the faculty for virtue or licence, between competing inclinations toward pleasure or the true) — evidencing the modest, bounded binary possibility Sytsma distinguishes from Alexander's absolute indeterminacy.

quote_evidence: ἡμεῖς δὲ τῆς λογικῆς φύσεώς φαμεν ὅλης κρατῆσαί ποτε τὸν λόγον καὶ μεταποιῆσαι πᾶσαν ψυχὴν εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ τελειότητα
rationale: Contra Celsum VIII.72 (corpus canonical_ref mislabeled '1.72'; text verified as CC VIII.72, SC 150): Origen asserts the Logos will one day master the WHOLE rational nature and transform EVERY soul into its own perfection, and that 'τὸ τέλος τῶν πραγμάτων ἀναιρεθῆναί ἐστι τὴν κακίαν' (the telos of things is the destruction of evil) — the key primary text for the fixed, foreordained cosmic telos Sytsma labels teleological predetermination, while preserving each soul's exousia.

quote_evidence: Nemo igitur quaerat efficientem causam malae uoluntatis; non enim est efficiens sed deficiens, quia nec illa effectio sed defectio.
rationale: De Civitate Dei XII.7.1 contains the literal causa efficiens/deficiens dictum the node quotes. NB: the node misattributes this sentence to De Lib. Arb. 2.20.54 — the verbatim wording is from De Civ. Dei XII.7, where Augustine restates the De Lib. Arb. doctrine.

quote_evidence: Motus ergo ille aversionis, quod fatemur esse peccatum, quoniam defectivus motus est, omnis autem defectus ex nihilo est, vide quo pertineat, et ad Deum non pertinere ne dubites.
rationale: De Lib. Arb. 2.20.54, the locus the node names: the will's aversio is a defectivus motus from nothing, not from God — the deficient-cause doctrine in its original De Lib. Arb. formulation (without the exact efficiens/deficiens sentence).

quote_evidence: quae peccata, ut iam diu disserimus, nonnisi propriae voluntati earum tribuenda sunt, nec ulla ulterior peccatorum causa quaerenda.
rationale: De Lib. Arb. 3.22.63, locus named by the node: sins are attributable only to propria voluntas and no further cause is to be sought — verbatim match to the node's claim.

quote_evidence: Aut igitur ipsa voluntas est prima causa peccandi, aut nullum peccatum est prima causa peccandi. Nec est cui recte imputetur peccatum nisi peccanti.
rationale: De Lib. Arb. 3.17.49 (node cites 3.17.48-49): the will itself is the first cause of sin and seeking a cause prior to will is illegitimate, preserving imputability — exactly the node's 'root of all evils is will / no prior cause' claim. (Note: 3.17.48 actually says radix omnium malorum is avaritia = improba voluntas, not the node's verbatim 'radicem omnium malorum esse voluntatem'.)

quote_evidence: quoniam peccaturum esse praesciverat, necesse erat id fieri, quod futurum esse praesciebat Deus. Quomodo est igitur voluntas libera ubi tam inevitabilis apparet necessitas?
rationale: De Lib. Arb. 3.2.4, the locus named: Evodius states the foreknowledge problem exactly as the node summarizes (foreknown sin was necessary, so how is the will free?).

quote_evidence: Sicut enim tu memoria tua non cogis facta esse quae praeterierunt; sic Deus praescientia sua non cogit facienda quae futura sunt.
rationale: De Lib. Arb. 3.4.11: the memory analogy the node quotes verbatim — memory does not compel past acts, so divine foreknowledge does not compel future ones.

quote_evidence: ita Deus neminem ad peccandum cogens, praevidet tamen eos qui propria voluntate peccabunt.
rationale: De Lib. Arb. 3.4.10 (node cites 3.4.10-11): foreknowledge is certainty of knowledge, not compulsion — God foresees those who will sin by their own will without forcing them. The human-foreknowledge thought experiment distinguishes epistemic certainty from causation, exactly the node's analysis. (The node's 3.5.14 quote 'mea voluntate futurum' is not in the 3.5.14 passage text and was not cited.)

quote_evidence: Virtutes igitur quibus recte vivitur, magna bona sunt: species autem quorumlibet corporum, sine quibus recte vivi potest, minima bona sunt: potentiae vero animi sine quibus recte vivi non potest, media bona sunt. Virtutibus nemo male utitur: caeteris autem bonis, id est, mediis et minimis, non solum bene, sed etiam male quisque uti potest.
rationale: De Lib. Arb. 2.19.50: the full magna/media/minima bona classification with the misuse criterion — the node's central claim verbatim. NB: the node locates the classification at 2.18.48; in the corpus text it stands at 2.19.50.

quote_evidence: sic liberam voluntatem sine qua nemo potest recte vivere, oportet et bonum, et divinitus datum, et potius eos damnandos qui hoc bono male utuntur, quam eum qui dederit dare non debuisse fatearis.
rationale: De Lib. Arb. 2.18.48: free will is a genuine good given by God even though it can be misused (hand/eye analogy) — supports the node's anti-Manichaean point that will itself is good and blame falls on misuse.

quote_evidence: Intueris enim iustitiam, qua nemo male utitur. Haec inter summa bona quae in ipso sunt homine numeratur, omnesque virtutes animi quibus ipsa recta vita et honesta constat.
rationale: De Lib. Arb. 2.18.50: virtues are summa bona that no one can misuse — the contrast class that makes will a 'middle' good in the node's hierarchy.

quote_evidence: Ignorantia vero et difficultas si naturalis est, inde incipit anima proficere, et ad cognitionem et requiem, donec in ea perficiatur vita beata, promoveri. Quem profectum in studiis optimis atque pietate, quorum facultas ei non negata est, si propria voluntate neglexerit, iuste in graviorem, quae iam poenalis est, ignorantiam difficultatemque praecipitatur
rationale: De Lib. Arb. 3.22.64: the core natural-vs-penal distinction with the node's exact terms (naturalis, propria voluntate neglexerit, poenalis, inde incipit anima proficere) and the infant-speech analogy later in the same passage. NB: the node's quote 'Si autem ista ignorantia et difficultas naturalis est' attributed to 3.20.55 actually corresponds to this 3.22.64 text.

quote_evidence: Creator vero eius ubique laudatur, vel quod eam ab ipsis exordiis ad summi boni capacitatem inchoaverit, vel quod eius profectum adiuvet, vel quod impleat proficientem atque perficiat
